questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between an object, a field, and a record, and how a custom object differs from a standard one?
options: An object defines the shape (fields) that every record of that type shares; a custom object behaves identically to a standard object once created, except its API name ends in __c and, unlike most standard objects, it can be deleted.

An object defines the shape (fields) that every record of that type shares; a custom object behaves identically to a standard object once created, except its API name ends in __c, though unlike a standard object it can never be deleted.
A field is one saved instance of an object, and a record is one property every instance shares.
A record defines the shape every field of that type shares, and an object is one saved instance of that shape.
Custom objects can hold fields and relationships, but unlike standard objects they can never appear in a report.
Standard and custom objects are functionally different — a custom object cannot have page layouts or related lists the way a standard object can.
questions.explain: An object defines a shape every record of that type shares. Once a custom object exists, it behaves exactly like a standard one — same tabs, fields, relationships, and reports — except its API name ends in __c, it was admin-defined, and it can be deleted, unlike most standard objects.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because it correctly states the API-name difference, but then flips the deletability fact — a custom object CAN be deleted, unlike most standard objects, not the other way around. That one swapped detail is the error.

questions.prompt: By default, what is the only field required to save a new Account record, per Lesson 3?
options: Account Name
Account Name and Billing Address
Account Name and Industry
Nothing — every field on Account is optional by default
questions.explain: The New Account form has dozens of available fields, but in a default org only Account Name is actually required to save the record — everything else is detail that can be filled in over time.

questions.prompt: A Lead is converted with the "Don't create an opportunity upon conversion" box checked. Per Lesson 4, what does that conversion still create?
options: A new or linked Account and a new or linked Contact
Only a new Contact, with no Account created at all
Only a new Account, with no Contact created at all
Nothing — checking that box cancels the entire conversion
questions.explain: Convert typically creates a new Account, a new Contact, and (optionally) a new Opportunity. Checking the box to skip the Opportunity only removes that third piece — the Account and Contact are still created or linked.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Lead, Opportunity, and Case, per Lesson 4.
options: A Lead has its own Status field and Activity timeline, kept separate from Account, Contact, and Opportunity until it's converted.
An Opportunity's defining feature is its stage, shown as a path moving toward Closed Won or Closed Lost.
A Case can be reassigned to a different rep or a queue using Change Owner.
Once a Lead is converted, the original Lead record is deleted entirely, leaving no trace it ever existed.
An Opportunity cannot carry an Amount or a Close Date — only a Quote can hold that information.
questions.explain: Leads are deliberately siloed until converted, with their own Status and timeline. An Opportunity's stage path, Amount, and Close Date are what make pipeline reporting possible — Amount and Close Date live directly on the Opportunity. A converted Lead becomes read-only, not deleted, and Cases are reassigned via Change Owner.

questions.prompt: Why can't a brand-new Product be added to an Opportunity the moment it's created, before anyone has touched a Price Book, per Lesson 5?
options: Every Product must have a Price Book Entry — a price linking it to a Price Book — before it can be sold anywhere, and a brand-new Product has none yet.
A Product can only be added to an Opportunity after its first Quote has been generated and emailed to a customer.
Opportunities can only hold Products that have already been purchased by at least one other customer.
Products require an External ID before they can appear on any Opportunity's line items.
questions.explain: A Product alone has no price — the Price Book Entry is what actually sets a price by linking a Product to a Price Book. Every Product must have an entry in at least the Standard Price Book before it can be sold anywhere.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the specific record that links one Product to one Price Book at a specific price is called a ________.
questions.explain: A Price Book Entry is the record that actually sets a price — it's why pricing is a separate layer from the Product itself, since the same product can have more than one price depending on which Price Book it's sold from.

questions.prompt: A rep books a 30-minute product demo with a prospect for next Thursday at 2 PM. Per Lesson 6, should that be logged as a Task or an Event, and why?
options: An Event, because it has a specific start and end time rather than just a single due date.
A Task, because every scheduled meeting is logged as a to-do item with a due date.
Either one works identically, since Task and Event store exactly the same fields.
Neither — demos aren't tracked by the Activity Timeline at all.
questions.explain: An Event is something on the calendar with a Start and an End date/time — exactly what a 30-minute demo booked for a specific slot needs. A Task has only a single Due Date, which fits a to-do item, not a scheduled block of time.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 7, which of these is an actual difference between a custom object and a standard object once the custom object is created?
options: Its API name ends in __c, and unlike most standard objects, it can be deleted.
It can't have page layouts — only a single default layout shared by every user.
It can't appear in reports, since reporting is reserved for standard objects.
It can't have relationships to other objects, only to other custom objects.
questions.explain: Once created, a custom object behaves exactly like a standard one — same tabs, page layouts, relationships, and reporting. The only real differences are the __c API name suffix, who defined it, and that it can be deleted.

questions.prompt: Match each section of an object's settings rail, per Lesson 8, to what it controls.
right: What columns show in list views and search results
Different field sets/picklist values for different business processes
How fields are arranged on the record page
The object's fields and its relationships to other objects
questions.explain: Fields & Relationships lists an object's fields and relationships. Page Layouts controls how fields are arranged on the record page. Record Types controls which field sets/picklist values apply to a given business process. Search Layouts controls what columns show in list views and search results.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of reaching any object's settings, per Lesson 8, in the correct order.
items: Click Setup (the gear icon, top right)
Open Object Manager, which lists every object
Click the specific object's name to open its settings
Use the left-hand settings rail to reach Fields & Relationships, Page Layouts, or Record Types
questions.explain: The path to any object's settings never changes: Setup, then Object Manager's full object list, then the specific object, and only then the settings rail that's identical across every object, standard or custom.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, why does the Step 1 data-type choice matter more than almost any other decision when creating a new field?
options: A field's data type is largely locked in once saved — Salesforce allows only narrow conversions later, so a Number field can't later become a Lookup Relationship.
The data type can always be changed freely later, so Step 1 is really just a formatting preference.
Step 1 only affects the field's label, not how the field actually behaves.
Data type only matters for custom fields — standard fields have no data-type restriction at all.
questions.explain: Unlike a field's label or help text, its data type is largely locked in once saved. Salesforce allows some narrow conversions (Text to Picklist, for instance), but a Number field can never become a Lookup Relationship after the fact.

questions.prompt: A Text field was created with a Length of 20, and users keep hitting save errors entering full addresses. Per Lesson 10, what's the fix?
options: Edit the existing field's Length setting to a larger value — no new field is required.
Delete the field and recreate it as a Checkbox, since Checkbox has no length limit.
Nothing can be done — a Text field's Length is permanently fixed once created.
Create a second Text field with a longer Length and leave the original field unused but still present.
questions.explain: A Text field's Length is a setting on the existing field, not a permanent lock on the field type itself — editing it to a larger character count fixes the save error without creating any new field.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what "Restrict picklist to the values defined in the value set" actually does, per Lesson 11?
options: When checked, it blocks the API, automation, and integrations from writing any value not on the list; when left unchecked, the UI still restricts users, but the API does not.

When checked, it blocks users in the UI from typing an off-list value; when left unchecked, the API, automation, and every integration still restrict every single write to the list, but the UI itself does not.
It has no real effect on data integrity — it only changes whether the picklist values display alphabetically.
It only applies to Picklist (Multi-Select) fields, never to a plain single-value Picklist.
It permanently deletes any value typed that isn't on the official list, rather than blocking the save.
It's required before a picklist field can be marked as an External ID.
questions.explain: Checking "Restrict picklist to the values defined in the value set" is a real data integrity guardrail — it blocks the API, automation, and integrations from writing an off-list value. Left unchecked, the UI still restricts users, but the API does not.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because it names the same two sides — UI and API — but swaps which one stays restricted when the box is unchecked. The lesson is explicit that leaving the box unchecked still restricts the UI, while the API is the side that becomes unrestricted — the opposite of what option B claims.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Picklist (Multi-Select) is the right choice only when "more than one value at a time" is a genuine, expected answer — for example, a Product's available ________ — while a plain Picklist is correct for a field like Stage or Status, where a record is usually in exactly one state at a time.
questions.explain: Lesson 11 gives a Product's available Certifications as the example where more than one value at once is a genuine, expected answer — exactly the case Picklist (Multi-Select) is built for.

questions.prompt: Why can't a Formula field ever hold a value that's out of date, the way a manually-entered Number field could, per Lesson 12?
options: A Formula field's value is computed fresh from its source fields every time the record is viewed — it's never stored, so there's nothing to go stale.
Formula fields are automatically re-saved by a background job every five minutes.
Formula fields can only reference fields that themselves never change.
A Formula field stores its value just like a Number field, but Salesforce validates it on every page load.
questions.explain: A Formula field stores nothing — Salesforce recalculates it from scratch every time the record is viewed, using whatever the source fields hold at that moment. There's nothing to go stale because there's nothing stored in the first place.

questions.prompt: This Opportunity is linked to an Account with 500 employees, and its own Amount is 50000. What does this formula field evaluate to?
options: FALSE, because AND() requires both conditions to be true, and Account.NumberOfEmployees > 1000 is false at 500 employees.
TRUE, because Amount > 10000 is true, and that alone is enough to satisfy AND().
TRUE, because AND() only requires at least one of its two conditions to hold.
An error, because a formula field can't reference a field on a related Account.
questions.explain: AND() returns TRUE only when every argument is true. Account.NumberOfEmployees > 1000 is false at 500 employees, so the whole formula evaluates to FALSE even though Amount > 10000 is true on its own.

questions.prompt: A field needs to show the most expensive related child record's Amount on its parent. Per Lesson 13, which summary type answers that, and on which side of the relationship is the Roll-Up Summary field created?
options: MAX, and the field is created on the master (parent) object, summarizing the detail (child) records.
MAX, and the field is created on the detail (child) object, summarizing the master (parent) record.
SUM, and the field is created on the detail (child) object.
COUNT, and the field is created on the master (parent) object.
questions.explain: MAX finds the largest value of a field across all child records. Roll-Up Summary fields are always created on the master side of a master-detail relationship, summarizing records from the detail side.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Required, Unique, and External ID, per Lesson 14.
options: A Required field is enforced everywhere a record can be created or edited — the UI, the API, an import, and a Flow.
Only certain field types, like Text, Number, Email, and Auto Number, can be marked Unique.
Checking External ID makes a field usable as the matching key in an upsert operation.
Required and Unique are the exact same property, just under two different names.
A Unique field rejects a duplicate value the same way regardless of whether case-sensitive or case-insensitive matching is chosen.
questions.explain: Required blocks a blank save everywhere a record can be written. Unique is only available on certain field types, and External ID is what makes a field usable as an upsert match key. Required and Unique are distinct properties, and case-sensitive versus case-insensitive uniqueness genuinely changes whether "ABC123" and "abc123" count as duplicates.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an operation that updates an existing record if a match is found on its External ID, or inserts a new record if no match exists, is called an ________.
questions.explain: An upsert gives the object, the External ID field to match on, and a batch of records — Salesforce finds existing matches and updates them, and inserts everything else, without creating duplicates.

questions.prompt: Match each property, per Lesson 15, to how it differs between a standard field and a custom field.
right: Editable on both standard and custom fields
Fixed by Salesforce on a standard field; chosen once at creation on a custom field
Always ends in __c on a custom field; no such suffix on a standard field
Almost never possible on a standard field; allowed on a custom field
questions.explain: A standard field's data type is fixed by Salesforce, while a custom field's is chosen once at creation. API names differ by the __c suffix. Deleting is almost never possible on a standard field but allowed on custom fields. Labels are editable on both.

questions.prompt: A detail record's related master is deleted. Per Lesson 16, what happens to the detail record under a Master-Detail relationship, and would the answer differ under a Lookup?
options: The detail record is deleted along with its master; under a Lookup, the related record would NOT be deleted — it would simply lose that reference.
The detail record is unaffected either way, since deleting a parent never affects related child records in Salesforce.
The detail record is deleted under both Master-Detail and Lookup — the relationship type makes no difference to delete behavior.
Under Master-Detail, the detail record becomes the new master; under Lookup, it's deleted.
questions.explain: Master-Detail is a tight bond: the detail record can't exist without its master, so deleting the master deletes every detail record with it. Lookup is deliberately loose — deleting a parent under a Lookup does not delete the related child record.

questions.prompt: A Lookup Filter on a Case's Contact field restricts choices to contacts whose Account matches the Case's own Account. Per Lesson 16, what problem does this actually solve?
options: It keeps a support rep from accidentally linking a Case to a Contact at the wrong company.
It prevents the Case from ever being reassigned to a different owner.
It automatically creates a new Contact if none match the filter.
It converts the Lookup Relationship into a Master-Detail Relationship.
questions.explain: A Lookup Filter narrows which records are even selectable in a lookup field. Comparing Contact: Account ID to Case: Account ID keeps a rep from linking a Case to a Contact at the wrong company — it has nothing to do with ownership or relationship type.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 17, why does a junction object need two Master-Detail relationships rather than one Master-Detail and one ordinary Lookup?
options: Only Master-Detail cascades deletes and controls sharing; if one side were a Lookup, deleting that parent wouldn't remove the junction record, leaving an orphaned reference with no sharing inherited from that side.
A junction object is only allowed to have Master-Detail fields at all — Lookup fields are technically disallowed on any custom object.
Two Master-Details are required because Salesforce charges extra API calls for a junction object with only one.
It doesn't actually matter — one Master-Detail and one Lookup produce an identical many-to-many result in every respect.
questions.explain: Master-Detail is what cascades deletes and controls sharing (Lesson 16). If one side of a junction object were a Lookup instead, deleting that parent wouldn't remove the junction record — it would leave an orphaned, un-shared reference, which defeats the point of the pattern.

questions.prompt: A requirement asks you to let a custom object reference "its own parent of the same type" — not specifically Users. Per Lesson 18, which relationship type do you reach for, and why can't Hierarchical do the job here?
options: An ordinary self-referencing Lookup, because Hierarchical Relationship is only available on the User object.
Hierarchical Relationship, because it's available on every object that needs to model a parent-of-the-same-type chain.
External Lookup Relationship, because any self-referencing relationship must point outside the org.
Master-Detail, because only Master-Detail can reference the same object it's defined on.
questions.explain: Hierarchical Relationship is restricted to the User object specifically. For any other object that needs to reference its own parent of the same type, like Campaign's Parent Campaign field, an ordinary self-referencing Lookup is the right tool.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: unlike a standard Lookup, which matches on a Salesforce record ID, an External Lookup Relationship matches against an ________ field — a value that identifies the record in the outside system.
questions.explain: An External Lookup Relationship connects to an External Object by matching on an External ID field rather than a Salesforce record ID, since the related record doesn't actually live inside Salesforce's own storage.

questions.prompt: Two Account records use the same Account object and the same Type field. One shows only partner-related Type values; the other shows the full customer list. Per Lesson 19, what single piece of configuration explains the difference?
options: Each Account was created under a different Record Type, and each Record Type narrows the picklist's available values independently.
The two Accounts must be on two entirely different objects, since Type's values can't vary on the same object.
One Account has the Type field marked Required, and the other doesn't.
The difference comes from two different page layouts alone — Record Types have nothing to do with picklist values.
questions.explain: A Record Type lets the same object and the same field expose a different subset of its full value list depending on which Record Type a record was created under — exactly how a Partner-flavored Account shows a narrower Type list than a Customer-flavored one.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 20, select every statement that describes a genuine schema-design warning sign worth a second look.
options: An object that isn't naturally central to the business has relationship lines radiating out to a dozen other objects.
A field is called "Close Date" on one object and "Closed On" on another object, meaning the same thing.
Master-Detail was chosen for a relationship specifically because a Roll-Up Summary would be convenient, without considering the cascading delete it also locks in.
A standard object was reused, with a Record Type and a few custom fields, instead of building a brand-new custom object.
questions.explain: A dense fan of relationships on a non-central object, inconsistent naming for the same concept, and picking Master-Detail for convenience without weighing its cascading delete are exactly the warning signs Lesson 20 names. Reusing a standard object with a Record Type and custom fields is the recommended practice, not a warning sign.

questions.prompt: You've inherited an org and need to understand how five custom objects relate before making a change. Per Lesson 21, would you start in Object Manager or Schema Builder, and why?
options: Schema Builder, because it's built for understanding structure — objects, fields, and relationships drawn as connected cards — rather than editing field by field.
Object Manager, because it's the only place relationships between objects are visible at all.
Either one works identically for this purpose, since both show the exact same canvas view.
Neither — relationships between custom objects can only be understood by reading Apex code.
questions.explain: Object Manager is where you create fields and relationships; Schema Builder is read-first by design, built specifically to answer "how does this object connect to everything else" fast — exactly what's needed before understanding five related custom objects.

questions.prompt: An integration imports a list of record IDs from a spreadsheet, and several fail to match any record. The IDs are 15 characters long, and the spreadsheet software is known to auto-capitalize text. Per Lesson 22, what's the most likely cause, and what would have prevented it?
options: The 15-character ID is case-sensitive, so auto-capitalization silently changed several IDs to point at the wrong record or none at all; the 18-character, case-insensitive ID would have prevented it.
The IDs are too short regardless of case — only 18-character IDs are ever valid for a Salesforce record.
The key prefix must have been wrong, since that's the only part of an ID that's case-sensitive.
Auto-capitalization has no effect on Salesforce IDs at all, so the failures must be unrelated to the spreadsheet.
questions.explain: The 15-character ID is case-sensitive — changing even one character's case points to a different record or none at all. The 18-character form adds characters encoding the original case, making it safe for exactly this kind of silent normalization.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of designing a data model from a plain-English requirement, per Lesson 23, in the correct order.
items: Find the nouns in the requirement, and check whether a standard object already covers each one
Identify the one concept with no standard-object match, and create a custom object only for that
Pick a relationship type for each connection based on the delete and sharing behavior it implies
Build a junction object with two Master-Detail relationships for any genuine many-to-many connection
Read the finished model back on a Schema Builder canvas to confirm the shape makes sense
questions.explain: The method runs: find the nouns and check reuse first, create a custom object only for what's left over, choose each relationship type deliberately, build a junction object wherever the connection is genuinely many-to-many, and verify the finished shape visually before shipping it.
